questions.stem: The mean monthly income of all 2,500 households in a town is ₹32,000, while a random sample of $100$ of those households has a mean income of ₹30,400. Which description is correct?
options: ₹32,000 is a statistic and ₹30,400 is a parameter
Both figures are parameters because both describe incomes
₹32,000 is a parameter and ₹30,400 is a statistic
Both figures are statistics because both are averages
questions.explanation: A parameter describes the whole population, here all 2,500 households, so ₹32,000 is a parameter. A statistic is computed from a sample, here the $100$ households, so ₹30,400 is a statistic. The two differ because a sample mean varies from sample to sample.

optionRationale.1: This reverses the roles; the figure for the whole population is the parameter.
optionRationale.2: Only the figure computed for the entire population is a parameter; the sample figure is a statistic.
optionRationale.4: Being an average does not decide the matter; what counts is whether the group is the whole population or a sample.

questions.objective: Distinguish a population parameter from a sample statistic

questions.stem: A school has $600$ boys and $400$ girls. A sample of $50$ students is drawn by proportional stratified sampling, with boys and girls as the two strata. How many girls are in the sample?
questions.explanation: In proportional stratified sampling each stratum is represented in the same proportion as in the population. Girls form $400/1000 = 40\%$ of the students, so the sample contains $40\%$ of $50 = 20$ girls and $30$ boys.

optionRationale.1: $25$ would be an equal split, which ignores the unequal stratum sizes.
optionRationale.2: $30$ is the number of boys in the sample, which has $60\%$ boys.
optionRationale.4: $40$ is the percentage of girls, not a count out of $50$.

questions.objective: Allocate a sample proportionally across strata

questions.stem: A population has standard deviation $\sigma = 18$. A researcher wants the standard error of the sample mean to be $1.5$. What sample size is required?
questions.explanation: The standard error is $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$. Setting $18/\sqrt{n} = 1.5$ gives $\sqrt{n} = 12$, hence $n = 144$. Squaring is essential: halving or similar manipulations of $\sigma$ alone do not give the sample size.

optionRationale.2: $12$ is $\sqrt{n}$, not $n$; the square root has not been undone.
optionRationale.3: $216$ comes from $18^2/1.5$, which mis-handles the square root.
optionRationale.4: $24$ has no link with $(\sigma/\text{SE})^2$; it comes from doubling $12$.

questions.objective: Find the sample size for a required standard error

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): If the p-value of a test is $0.03$, the null hypothesis is rejected at the $5\%$ level of significance.
Reason (R): A p-value of $0.03$ means that the probability that the null hypothesis is true is $3\%$.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true but (R) is false.
(A) is false but (R) is true.
questions.explanation: Since $0.03 < 0.05$, the result is significant at the $5\%$ level and $H_0$ is rejected, so A is true. The p-value, however, is the probability of data at least this extreme when $H_0$ is assumed true; it is not the probability that $H_0$ itself is true, so R is false.

optionRationale.1: R is false, so it cannot explain A; the p-value is computed assuming $H_0$ is true.
optionRationale.2: R is not true, so the pair is not 'both true'.
optionRationale.4: A is true because $0.03$ is below the $0.05$ cut-off.

questions.stem: Match each term of hypothesis testing in List-I with its meaning in List-II.

right: I. Rejecting $H_0$ when $H_0$ is actually true
II. Failing to reject $H_0$ when $H_0$ is actually false
III. The largest probability of a Type I error the tester will accept
IV. The set of test-statistic values that lead to rejection of $H_0$

options: A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV
A-I, B-II, C-IV, D-III
A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV
A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV
questions.explanation: A Type I error is a false rejection of a true $H_0$ (I). A Type II error is a failure to reject a false $H_0$ (II). The level of significance $\alpha$ is the maximum Type I error probability that is tolerated (III). The critical region is the set of statistic values that triggers rejection (IV).

optionRationale.1: Items A and B have been interchanged; check each pairing against its definition.
optionRationale.2: Items C and D have been interchanged; check each pairing against its definition.
optionRationale.3: Items A and C have been interchanged; check each pairing against its definition.

questions.objective: Match error types and the critical region with their meanings

questions.stem: The tensile strengths (in kg) of $8$ cables are $62, 65, 61, 66, 64, 67, 63, 68$. To test $H_0: \mu = 60$ with the one-sample t-test, the value of the t statistic is closest to
questions.explanation: The sample mean is $64.5$ and the sample variance is $\sum(x-\bar{x})^2/(n-1) = 42/7 = 6$, so $s = \sqrt{6} \approx 2.449$. Then $t = (64.5 - 60)/(s/\sqrt{8}) = 4.5/0.866 \approx 5.20$ with $7$ degrees of freedom.

optionRationale.1: This uses the divisor $n$ instead of $n-1$ in the standard deviation, which overstates $t$.
optionRationale.3: This leaves out the $\sqrt{n}$ and divides the difference $4.5$ by $s$ only.
optionRationale.4: This divides by $s/n$ instead of $s/\sqrt{n}$, which inflates the statistic.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about degrees of freedom in t-tests.
A. A one-sample t-test on $12$ observations has $11$ degrees of freedom.
B. A paired t-test on $10$ pairs of observations has $9$ degrees of freedom.
C. A pooled two-sample t-test with sample sizes $7$ and $9$ has $16$ degrees of freedom.
D. Degrees of freedom do not change the critical value of a t-test.
Choose the correct answer.
options: A and B only
A and C only
B, C and D only
A, B and C only
questions.explanation: A one-sample test uses $n-1 = 11$ and a paired test works on the $10$ differences, so it uses $10-1 = 9$; A and B are true. The pooled test uses $n_1 + n_2 - 2 = 7 + 9 - 2 = 14$, not $16$, so C is false. Critical values of t shrink as the degrees of freedom grow, so D is false.

optionRationale.3: A is true, so a set that excludes it cannot be right; C and D are false too.
optionRationale.4: C is false, since the pooled degrees of freedom are $14$.

questions.objective: State the degrees of freedom for common t-tests

questions.stem: A sample of $16$ bulbs has mean life $24.5$ months and standard deviation $s = 2$ months. For $H_0: \mu = 23.5$ the t statistic has $15$ degrees of freedom. The critical value is $2.131$ for a two-tailed test at $5\%$ and $1.753$ for a right-tailed test at $5\%$. Which conclusion is correct?
options: H₀ is rejected in the two-tailed test but not rejected in the right-tailed test
H₀ is rejected in both tests
H₀ is not rejected in either test
H₀ is not rejected in the two-tailed test but is rejected in the right-tailed test
questions.explanation: The statistic is $t = (24.5 - 23.5)/(2/\sqrt{16}) = 1/0.5 = 2.00$. Since $2.00 < 2.131$ the two-tailed test does not reject $H_0$, but $2.00 > 1.753$ so the right-tailed test does. The choice of alternative changes the critical value and so the decision.

optionRationale.1: The comparison is reversed: $2.00$ is below $2.131$ but above $1.753$.
optionRationale.2: $2.00$ is not above $2.131$, so the two-tailed test cannot reject.
optionRationale.3: $2.00$ exceeds the one-tailed value $1.753$, so rejection does occur in that test.

questions.objective: Compare a t statistic with one-tailed and two-tailed critical values

questions.stem: Six students' scores before and after coaching are: before $72, 68, 75, 70, 66, 74$ and after $75, 70, 79, 71, 70, 77$. For the paired t-test of $H_0: \mu_d = 0$ the critical value at $5\%$ (two-tailed, $5$ degrees of freedom) is $2.571$. Which statement is correct?
options: $t \approx 5.94$ with $5$ degrees of freedom, so $H_0$ is not rejected at $5\%$
$t \approx 5.94$ with $6$ degrees of freedom, so $H_0$ is rejected at $5\%$
$t \approx 5.94$ with $5$ degrees of freedom, so $H_0$ is rejected at $5\%$
$t \approx 2.43$ with $5$ degrees of freedom, so $H_0$ is not rejected at $5\%$
questions.explanation: The differences (after minus before) are $3, 2, 4, 1, 4, 3$, with mean $2.833$ and standard deviation $s_d \approx 1.169$. Then $t = 2.833/(1.169/\sqrt{6}) \approx 5.94$ with $n - 1 = 5$ degrees of freedom. As $5.94 > 2.571$, $H_0$ is rejected.

optionRationale.1: The statistic is correct, but $5.94 > 2.571$, so the conclusion should be rejection.
optionRationale.2: A paired test on $6$ pairs has $5$ degrees of freedom, not $6$.
optionRationale.4: The value $2.43$ does not arise from these differences; the correct statistic is far larger.

questions.stem: Two independent samples of yields are $12, 15, 14, 16, 13$ (machine P) and $10, 12, 11, 9, 13, 10$ (machine Q). Assuming equal population variances, the pooled two-sample t statistic for $H_0: \mu_P = \mu_Q$ is closest to
questions.explanation: The means are $14$ and $10.83$ and the sample variances are $2.5$ and $2.167$. The pooled variance is $(4\cdot2.5 + 5\cdot2.167)/9 = 2.315$. Then $t = 3.167/\sqrt{2.315(1/5 + 1/6)} \approx 3.167/0.921 \approx 3.44$ with $9$ degrees of freedom.

optionRationale.1: This forgets the square root over the pooled variance times $(1/n_1 + 1/n_2)$.
optionRationale.3: This takes the square root of the pooled variance only and multiplies it by $(1/5 + 1/6)$.
optionRationale.4: This divides by $s_p$ alone and leaves out the factor $\sqrt{1/n_1 + 1/n_2}$.

questions.objective: Compute a pooled two-sample t statistic
